idiom_name: decision function whose fall-through is denial, over an explicit grant set
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: every protected operation passes a single decision; the decision searches an explicit grant set (roles, capabilities, ACL entries, policy rules) and answers 'permitted' only on a match. Everything else - no matching grant, no identifiable subject, an operation or resource the decision cannot classify, or an error inside the lookup - produces 'denied'. Put the default in the structure rather than in a convention: an unmatched route in the router, an unlisted operation in the policy, an unhandled case in the decision's switch, an unconfigured endpoint under a fallback policy. Make the failure direction uniform (any error, timeout or unparseable policy means deny and is logged with its reason), protect the decision point so every path reaches it, and keep the grant set small enough to review - a default is only as safe as the list of things it admits.
pitfalls: Turning the default into a convention ('remember to call the guard') instead of a structural property (an unconfigured route, operation or handler is denied).
Failing open on the error path: a timeout, exception or parse failure inside the lookup must deny, not continue.
Grants wider than intended (wildcards, any-authenticated, admin-for-services) recreate a permissive default at a coarser level.
Denials that are neither logged nor distinguishable from 'no rule', so misconfiguration is discovered by users and fixed by widening access.

Authentication mistaken for authorization: returning 'permitted' because the caller's identity was verified (valid JWT, successful login) without checking that the identity carries an explicit grant for the operation — the single most common authorisation failure pattern.

TOCTOU between decision and use: the grant is confirmed, but the caller's effective attributes (tenant, role, resource ownership) change before the operation executes, so a permission checked on an old self is exercised by a new self.

Implicit grant inheritance: adding a principal to a broad group to clear a 403 widens every other member's effective permission set simultaneously, making targeted revocation impossible without group restructuring.

Treating 'internal' as an implicit grant: a service call that works because both endpoints are in the same cluster or VPC is not evidence of an explicit grant — it is a missing check, and a compromised container can reach any other internal service.

Default-deny at one layer while another layer permits: a deny-by-default application policy over a permissive network ACL means the network layer is the real access control, and it can be bypassed by tunnelling or address spoofing.

Failing to audit the positive model: the deny-by-default guarantee only holds as long as the grant set is reviewed; accumulated wildcards, generated rules and inherited roles silently erode the default into a de-facto allowlist.

Bypassing the decision point through a different entry path: the application enforces default-deny on its API layer but a direct database connection string or an admin console endpoint bypasses the same decision point — the grant set is only as strong as its narrowest bypass.

Stale grant accumulation: the allowlist grows over time as operators add wildcard entries to clear 403s, making the effective grant set wider than the security model intended without any single change being obviously dangerous — regular automated scanning for over-wide grants is the only reliable mitigation.

Overly broad break-glass procedures: a documented emergency access path that grants 'admin access' or 'access to all resources' for any incident creates a standing invitation that attackers target; break-glass grants must be narrowly scoped (one resource, one operation, one principal, one time window) to avoid hollowing out the default.

Assuming the cloud provider's defaults are secure: many cloud services (S3 buckets, RDS instances, Elasticsearch clusters) are secure by default in new accounts but become insecure when cross-account sharing or public exposure is enabled for convenience and never reviewed back to the minimum necessary.

Missing the human factor: an operator who has never seen a deny-by-default system habituates to widening grants to clear legitimate access requests — training, monitoring of grant-widening events, and treating each 403 as a signal rather than an error prevents the slow erosion of the positive model.

Wrong move: making every layer and every operation fail closed uniformly -> a policy-store outage denies even low-risk reads the decision point could have served from a recent cached grant, and the incident gets 'fixed' with a global bypass that is never removed -> instead decide the failure direction per operation class: deny writes and privileged reads outright, serve low-risk reads only from a bounded, staleness-capped cached grant, and keep that cached path as narrow and audited as any grant.

Wrong move: switching default-deny on a live system in one step -> legitimate traffic 403s simultaneously, operators respond by reverting the policy or adding wildcards, and the resulting grant set ends up wider than before the exercise -> instead stage the rollout (log-only/dry-run mode first, then enforcement namespace by namespace or route group by route group, with denial-rate metrics reviewed before each step) so missing grants are found by telemetry instead of by users.

Wrong move: assuming the framework's shipped default is the safe default -> ASP.NET Core's FallbackPolicy is null until explicitly set, so endpoints carrying no authorization metadata stay anonymous even though the docs describe the fail-safe configuration -> instead configure and test the platform-level default (FallbackPolicy, anyRequest().denyAll(), a default-deny NetworkPolicy) as a deliverable in itself; a default nobody set is a default nobody verified.
